sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
Durham is unusual because it charges vehicles for entering part of the old city. As shown on the council's Road User Charge Zone page in October 2026, the charge is £5 a day between 10am and 2am, Monday to Sunday, except Christmas Day, Boxing Day and New Year's Day; an ANPR camera at Silver Street and Claypath records vehicles and an unpaid charge can bring a £50 Penalty Charge Notice [1]. In January 2025 the council was reported to be proposing to raise the charge from £2 to £5, add Sundays and bank holidays and extend enforcement from 10am-4pm to 10am-2am, citing disruptive parking, safety and air pollution and up to 30,000 vehicles a month through the area [0]. We found no dated source for the decision itself; the £5 charge comes only from the council page.

On-street rules have moved towards Sunday charging. A November 2023 report proposed Sunday tariffs on all on-street bays in Durham City, estimated at £119,890 extra income a year, noting that charging had run Monday to Saturday since 2003 [2]. On 20 February 2024 the Highways Committee endorsed the parking orders in principle: Sunday operation from 8am to 6pm and a 20p per hour rise, with the extra income to fund a Sunday Park and Ride service, against public objections about cost of living, businesses and visitor numbers [3]. The Controlled Parking Zone needs a permit from 8am to 6pm every day including bank holidays, with resident permits at £56 a year for the first and £84 for the second [15]. In June 2026 the council proposed changing which holidays are excluded from bay restrictions, with objections invited until 2 July 2026; the notice gives no charges or in-force date [16].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text: The main developments are in the park and ride and in the redevelopment around the Prince Bishops garage. The £2 million expansion of Sniperley Park and Ride, funded through the Transforming Cities Fund, was announced complete on 19 November 2024, adding 261 bays to reach 587 [8]. Belmont has 533 spaces and eight EV points and, according to the council, is open seven days [9]; Howlands Farm has 361 spaces and is open Monday to Saturday only [10]. The Prince Bishops Place redevelopment was approved in July 2024 with the multi-storey car park retained [12], and revised plans in February 2026 drop the hotel and raise student accommodation to around 500 rooms above the car park and shops, with a new planning application expected by the end of that month [13]. The report gives no space numbers. The Light, an off-street car park in DH1, was the subject of a council order made on 7 August 2026 with £1 an hour from 8am to 8pm on all days, though the notice's in-force date is inconsistent [11]. The University Hospital North Durham visitor car park moved to number-plate recognition from 1 May 2025 [14], and the council and the operator Zest announced 250 new charging locations across County Durham in July 2024, not specifically in the city [17].

sections.title: Operators, positioning and utilisation
sections.text:
Four car parks in the city are council-run pay-and-display: The Sands multi-storey (277 spaces), Sidegate (107), Providence Row (19) and Wharton Park (25); Prince Bishops, The Riverwalk, Walkergate and the LNER station are listed as third-party car parks without spaces or charges [7]. From 4 June 2026 Sidegate and The Sands moved from £1.80 for up to two hours then 80p an hour to £2.10 then £1.10, and Providence Row from 40p to 55p per half hour [5]; Wharton Park rose from 70p to 80p per half hour [6]. In March 2026 the Local Democracy Reporting Service reported increases from April of 30p an hour off-street and 15p on-street in Durham, and that the council said its centre charges were competitive with private operators [4].

Our data cover Prince Bishops (400 spaces), The Riverwalk (460), Sidegate (104) and three park-and-ride sites, from the regional open-data feed since late September 2026; the other four car parks in the feed have too few readings to use. The two third-party garages are far busier than the council's Sidegate. Prince Bishops averaged 35% on weekdays and 45% at weekends and reached 93% in a Saturday-noon reading; The Riverwalk averaged 24% and 22% and reached 79% on a Saturday; Sidegate, a council garage, averaged only 6% on weekdays, which is notable given that its price went up on 4 June [5]. The park-and-ride sites are very lightly used on weekdays: Belmont (533) averaged 3%, Howlands (357) 11% and Sniperley (326) 25%. Feed capacities differ somewhat from the council's: Sniperley is 326 in the feed against 587 after the 2024 expansion [8]. These are about four weeks of readings.
